You are helping a user write SQL queries to a database. If something is not clear, you can ask the user to clarify what they need. The schema for the database being accessed is the following:
        
CREATE TABLE conductor (
    Conductor_ID INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Name TEXT,
    Age INT,
    Nationality TEXT,
    Year_of_Work INT,
    UNIQUE (Conductor_ID)
);

CREATE TABLE orchestra (
    Orchestra_ID INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Orchestra TEXT,
    Conductor_ID INT,
    Record_Company TEXT,
    Year_of_Founded REAL,
    Major_Record_Format TEXT,
    UNIQUE (Orchestra_ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (Conductor_ID) REFERENCES conductor(Conductor_ID)
);

CREATE TABLE performance (
    Performance_ID INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Orchestra_ID INT,
    Type TEXT,
    Date TEXT,
    Official_ratings_(millions) REAL,
    Weekly_rank TEXT,
    Share TEXT,
    UNIQUE (Performance_ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (Orchestra_ID) REFERENCES orchestra(Orchestra_ID)
);

CREATE TABLE show (
    Show_ID INT,
    Performance_ID INT,
    If_first_show bool,
    Result TEXT,
    Attendance REAL,
    FOREIGN KEY (Performance_ID) REFERENCES performance(Performance_ID)
);

There isn’t a “famous” flag/column in this schema, so we need a definition (e.g., most performances, highest official ratings, biggest attendance, etc.). Here are a few common ways to interpret “famous conductors”:

**1) Conductors with the most performances (top 10)**
```sql
SELECT
  c.Conductor_ID,
  c.Name,
  c.Nationality,
  COUNT(p.Performance_ID) AS performance_count
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
JOIN performance p ON p.Orchestra_ID = o.Orchestra_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name, c.Nationality
ORDER BY performance_count DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

**2) Conductors with the highest total official ratings (top 10)**
```sql
SELECT
  c.Conductor_ID,
  c.Name,
  SUM(COALESCE(p."Official_ratings_(millions)", 0)) AS total_official_ratings_millions
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
JOIN performance p ON p.Orchestra_ID = o.Orchestra_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
ORDER BY total_official_ratings_millions DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

**3) Conductors with the highest total show attendance (top 10)**
```sql
SELECT
  c.Conductor_ID,
  c.Name,
  SUM(COALESCE(s.Attendance, 0)) AS total_attendance
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
JOIN performance p ON p.Orchestra_ID = o.Orchestra_ID
JOIN show s ON s.Performance_ID = p.Performance_ID
GROUP BY c.Conductor_ID, c.Name
ORDER BY total_attendance DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

Which definition of “famous” do you want (performances, ratings, attendance, or something else)?
just tell me some names of famous conductors

I can’t reliably list “famous” conductors from your database because the schema/data shown doesn’t include any field that marks someone as famous, and I don’t have your table contents.

If you want, I can pull the names from your `conductor` table (all of them), or derive “famous” as “most performances / highest ratings / biggest attendance” and return the top names using SQL. Which do you prefer?
Just pull names from the conductor table.

```sql
SELECT Name
FROM conductor
WHERE Name IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY Name;
```
Just keep in mind to only consider conductors based on their past conducting activities.

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT c.Name
FROM conductor c
JOIN orchestra o  ON o.Conductor_ID = c.Conductor_ID
JOIN performance p ON p.Orchestra_ID = o.Orchestra_ID
WHERE c.Name IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY c.Name;
```
